pages.text: Poku’s seat was empty again. Rashida picked up his exercise book from his desk and looked at the last page he had written. It was only half finished. “Where is he?” she asked the class. Nobody knew. After school, she carried his book to his house at the edge of town, where the road turned brown and the trees ended.

pages.alt: A girl carries a boy’s exercise book along a road that changes from green to brown and bare.

pages.text: She found Poku near the river, with a shovel and a bucket, beside men digging in a pit. His boots were caked in mud. “I am not coming back,” he said. “A day here pays more than my mother makes in a week. My little sister needs medicine and our rent is due.” His voice was not proud. It was tired. Rashida said nothing for a moment.

pages.text: Rashida told her class teacher, who called Mrs Osafo, the social welfare officer. Mrs Osafo did not scold. “Poku is not a bad boy,” she said. “He is a boy with a hard problem. Let us find out the facts, and see what we can do for him, and for his mother.” She visited Poku’s mother, sat on a low stool, and listened.

Let us find out the facts, and see what we can do for him, and for his mother.” She visited Poku’s mother, sat on a low stool, and listened.
pages.alt: A welfare officer sits with Poku’s mother at her small stall and listens with her notebook closed.

pages.text: “Here is what the law says,” said Mrs Osafo to Rashida and her teacher. “The Children’s Act, the Labour Act and the Human Trafficking Act protect children from dangerous work and from being taken to work in places like pits. International rules treat mining work for children as one of the worst forms of child labour. A child may not be made to do work that harms their health or stops their schooling.”
sentences: “Here is what the law says,” said Mrs Osafo to Rashida and her teacher.

International rules treat mining work for children as one of the worst forms of child labour.
A child may not be made to do work that harms their health or stops their schooling.”
pages.alt: A page of law titles, the Children’s Act, the Labour Act and the Human Trafficking Act, with a child’s drawing beside it.

pages.text: “How many children are doing this?” asked Rashida. “Nobody knows exactly,” said Mrs Osafo. “A report from UNICEF in 2022 estimated that between twenty and thirty thousand children in Ghana take part in mining-related work. The Minerals Commission counted more than five thousand six hundred directly involved, and NGOs say that is probably too low. Many are between twelve and seventeen, and some are as young as five.”

The Minerals Commission counted more than five thousand six hundred directly involved, and NGOs say that is probably too low.
Many are between twelve and seventeen, and some are as young as five.”
pages.alt: A chart with two bars, 20,000 to 30,000 and 5,600, and a question mark between them.

pages.text: “Why is it dangerous?” asked Rashida. “Pits can collapse, tools can injure, and children may handle mercury or cyanide without protection. They breathe dust and fumes, and they can lose years of school. Girls face extra risks, including being trafficked to mining sites under false promises. Our hearts go out to them, but our law must also protect them.” Rashida held Poku’s book tighter.

pages.text: Mrs Osafo did three things. She helped Poku’s mother apply for a small support grant and a loan for her stall. She spoke to the headteacher about school feeding and a place for Poku in the afternoon class. And she asked a local group to give Poku a weekend job at a vegetable farm, safe and lawful. “It will not fix everything,” she told the family. “But it is a path back.”

“But it is a path back.”
pages.alt: A welfare officer, a headteacher and a mother stand together by the school gate, with a vegetable garden behind them.

pages.text: A month later, Poku walked through the gate in his uniform. He looked thinner than before, but he was smiling. Rashida handed him his exercise book. “You still owe us half a page,” she said. Poku laughed. “I will finish it,” he said. That evening he wrote in the margin: “School is not a place I escape. It is a place that gives me back my future.” The end.

activities.question: Why did Poku stop coming to school?

He did not like his teacher

activities.prompt: Mrs Osafo listens before she acts. Why is that a good approach?
options: She learns the real problem and can find a fair answer

activities.question: What did Mrs Osafo do to help?
options: Support for the mother, a school place and safe weekend work
